title: A settings export a team can trust
metaTitle: Exports that say what the file is
excerpt: Tell people what an export contains, how fresh it is, and when it will arrive. A button labeled Export that produces nothing is a support ticket.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. The working desk fits a piece about an export a team can actually trust.
caption: The file should match the sentence on the screen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an export screen say before the download?
faqs.answer: What the file contains, what it leaves out, which records are in scope, and the format. If a filter is applied, say that the file matches the filter. If attachments are links that expire, say when they expire. The person should be able to explain the file to someone else without opening a help article.

faqs.question: How do you show that export data is fresh?
faqs.answer: Put a timestamp on the result and inside the file, as of the moment the snapshot was taken. If some columns update on a delay, name those columns and the delay. A nightly report can be useful, as long as the screen says it is last night's numbers and not a live copy.

faqs.question: What should happen after someone clicks Export?
faqs.answer: A small file can download immediately and still leave a line in an export history. A large file should show a job with states: queued, preparing, ready, or failed. Ready includes the download and the timestamp, and failed includes a sentence and a way to try again. A button that flickers and produces no record is unfinished.

markdown:
A data export ux tells the person what the file contains, how fresh the data is, and when the file will arrive. A button that says Export and then nothing is a support ticket. The team asked for a copy because they do not yet trust the product to be the only place the work lives. Meet that request with a file they can explain to someone else.

The export is a product surface, small and serious. Specify it the way you specify a screen people use every day. The difference is that this screen's job is to end in a file, and the file has to match the sentence you showed before they pressed the button.

## What the file contains

Say the contents before the click, in a list a founder can read to their finance lead or their lawyer without translating.

Name the objects. Projects, members, invoices, comments. If comments are excluded, say excluded. If attachments are links that expire, say they expire, and say when. A file that arrives without the attachments the sentence promised will be read as a broken promise, even if the rows themselves are perfect.

Name the format. A spreadsheet they can open, a JSON archive a developer can script, or both. If you offer both, say which one is the human copy and which one is the full archive. People choose the spreadsheet and then discover the archive had the rest. Put that fact next to the choice.

Name the scope. This workspace, this project, or the rows in the current filter. Filters are a common surprise. If the button exports only what is on screen, the label has to say so. "Export view" and "Export everything in this project" are different actions. Shipping only one of them is fine. Labeling one as the other is how a backup turns out to be a slice.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone leaves having learned enough to achieve their goal. The export screen is that test in miniature. After they read it, they should know what they will hold. If they still need a help article to learn whether attachments are included, the screen is unfinished.

## How fresh the data is

"Export" can mean three different clocks, and the screen should pick one out loud.

A snapshot as of the moment they pressed the button. This is the right default for a backup. Say "as of 14:02, your time" on the result, not only "today."

A report that was generated earlier, on a schedule. Nightly numbers are useful, and they are stale by lunch. Say when the snapshot was taken. Offering a fresh run is a separate action, with its own wait.

A file that streams live and might change while it is being built. Avoid this unless you have no choice. If a long export can miss a row written halfway through, say that the file is a point in time at the start of the job, and ignore writes that arrive later. Consistency beats a false sense of completeness.

Include the timestamp inside the file, in a header or a column, not only in the email. Files get detached from the message that delivered them. The founder who opens it next month should be able to see the freshness without finding the thread.

If some columns update on a delay, name those columns. "Revenue figures follow the accounting sync, which runs hourly" is a sentence that prevents a panicked re-export. Hide that delay and they will press the button three times.

## When it will arrive

Small exports can finish in the request, and the screen can offer the download immediately. Say that it is ready. Leave the file available if they navigate away, for a stated window.

Large exports should not trap the tab. Confirm that the job has started, say that you will keep it in a list, and say whether you will also send email. Give a range only if you have one you have measured. "Usually under ten minutes for a workspace this size" is allowed when it is true and you are willing to be wrong in public by showing the real status. "Instantly" is not a status.

The job needs states they can see: queued, preparing, ready, failed. Ready includes the download and the freshness time. Failed includes a sentence and a way to try again. A spinner with no state is the same support ticket as a button that does nothing.

Write the email, if you send one, as a receipt. What it contains, the timestamp, the link, and when the link stops working. The link should require the same login they already use. A public URL with a long secret is a file you have left in a hallway. Prefer a signed-in download, and say so, so nobody forwards the email expecting a stranger to open it.

If the job fails because the workspace is too large for the self-serve path, say that in the product and name the next step you actually offer. A generic failure after a ten-minute wait is how trust dies on a feature whose whole point is trust.

## A button that says Export and then nothing

The failure has a shape. They press the button. The button flickers. Nothing downloads. No email arrives. No record exists. They press it again. Support hears about it after the third try, usually on the day they needed the file for someone outside the company.

Build the receipt first. Even a fast export gets a line in an export history: who asked, what scope, when it finished, a link that still works. The history is how you prove the button did something, including to the person who clicked it and then doubted themselves.

Disable the double submit while a job for that scope is running, and point at the running job. Two identical files, started a second apart, look like a glitch even when both succeeded.

If the browser blocks the download, say so next to the button. A help sentence that appears only when the file did not start is more useful than a paragraph that is always on screen. Keep it short. "If the file did not download, check the browser's blocked downloads, or take it from the export history."

Empty exports are a result, not a bug to hide. "This project has no invoices yet, so the file would be empty. Export anyway, or cancel." An empty file with no warning looks like a broken report.

## What you owe the person who asked

They are often leaving, auditing, or handing work to an accountant. The tone can be plain. Skip the cheer. A receipt is the right genre.

Respect the permission. A member who cannot see billing should not be able to export billing, and the button should not appear and then fail. If an admin must approve the export, say that the request is waiting on a named role, and tell the admin. A silent queue is another version of a button that does nothing, relocated into someone else's inbox.

Deletion and export interact. If someone requests an export and closes the account the same day, the file still has to arrive, or the closing flow has to say that exports must finish first. Write that down so support is not inventing policy in the chat.

Sensitive columns need a choice when the audience varies. An export for a teammate might exclude customer emails. An export for the admin might include them. Offer the choice on the screen, with the default on the safer side, and echo the choice in the receipt. Do not bury it in a settings page they will not open on the way out.

## A check you can run this week

Ask for an export the way a skeptical founder would.

- Can you say what is in the file before you press the button?
- Does the result show a timestamp?
- If you leave the page, can you find the file again?
- Does a second click create a duplicate job or point at the first?
- Does a member without access see the button?
- Does the failed state say what to do?

Open the file. Check one relationship you care about, such as whether a comment is attached to the right project. A row count that matches, with the relationships scrambled, is still a failed export. The screen cannot catch every mapping bug, which is why the contents list has to be specific enough that a human can test it.

Keep the sample file you tested against. When the schema changes, update the sample and the sentence together. An export whose columns drift away from the label is the silent failure returning in a later release.

## After they have the file

The export history can stay quiet. It does not need a badge, a celebration, or a prompt to export every week. The people who need it will come back on the day they need it. Your job is to make that day short.

Keyboard use is the next gap on a product a team sits in all day. [Keyboard use on a product a team lives in](/blog/keyboard-use-on-a-product-a-team-lives-in) covers tab order, visible focus, and a shortcut for the action they repeat. An export buried in a menu they cannot reach without a pointer will be the button they never find.

When you want the receipt and the file specified with the rest of the interface, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The export is part of the product, especially on the day someone needs to leave with their data.
